Densify COMPLETE (PHYS 302–mid-323): dependent principle as Church testimony (pure/mixed) or extra-ecclesial; proof vs declaration; analytic vs dialectic rules; public/private principle (councils, symbols, confessions, private doctors); gentile testimony of Hermes/Sibyls with Casaubon's critique; Cap. 10 close via Eusebius on the Artemonites. source_text: CAPUT DECIMUM. De principio S.S. Theologiae a primo dependente & ad illud ordinato. Hactenus explicavimus primum sacrae Theologiae principium: sequitur dependens a primo, et ad illud ordinatum; quod ad primum, sacram videlicet scripturam, dirigendo rem aliquam credibilem facit, & ad credendum per declarationem aut probationem disponendo invitat.
english:
CHAPTER TEN
On the principle of sacred theology dependent on the first and ordered to it
So far we have explained the first principle of sacred theology.
There follows that which depends on the first and is ordered to it.
By directing some believable matter to Sacred Scripture as the first principle, it makes that matter credible.
By disposing the hearer through declaration or proof, it invites him to believe.

source_text:
Qui vero hodieque gentilium scriptis in negotio fidei plusculum deferunt cum Scholasticis & Jesuitis, his opponi debet, quod Eusebius lib. 5. cap. 28. de Artemonitis refert. Scripturas, inquiens, divinas absque ulla timoris Dei reverentia corruperunt: antiquae vero fidei regulam proterve & impie respuunt, ignorantes Christum, quem idcirco non inveniunt, quia non recte quaesiverunt. Et in tantum stultitiae impietatisque prolapsi sunt, ut, siquis eis sermonem de Scripturis proposuerit, illi e contrario opponant: utrum hic sermo, de quo agitur, conjunctum an separatum genus syllogismi faciat: et derelinquentes sanctas Dei scripturas geometriam tractant, tanquam qui vere de terra sint, de terra loquuntur: & ideo eum, qui de sursum est, ignorant. Denique Euclides apud eos vel maxime in Geometriae disciplinis viget. Sed & Aristoteles & Theophrastus ab his in admiratione habentur. Galenus vero a nonnullis eorum & adoratur. Qui earum artibus & doctrinis haereseos suae impietatem nituntur asserere: & deceptionibus hominum ignorantium Deum, simplicitatem divinarum scripturarum, & sinceritatem fidei subruunt. Sed haec faciunt, quia nec vicini facti sunt fidei, propterea & divinas scripturas absque ullo timore contemerant, & corrumpentes eas emendare se dicunt.

[Cap. 10 COMPLETE. CAPUT UNDECIMUM / De S. Theologiae distributione begins PHYS 323.]
english: But those who still today defer somewhat more to gentile writings in the business of faith, with the Scholastics and Jesuits — to these ought to be opposed what Eusebius (book 5, chapter 28) reports concerning the Artemonites: They have corrupted the divine Scriptures, he says, without any reverence of the fear of God; and they boldly and impiously reject the rule of the ancient faith, being ignorant of Christ, whom therefore they do not find, because they have not sought rightly. And they have so far slipped into folly and impiety that, if someone proposes to them a discourse from the Scriptures, they on the contrary oppose: whether this discourse under discussion makes a conjoined or a separated genus of syllogism; and abandoning God's holy Scriptures they treat geometry — as those who truly are of the earth, they speak of the earth; and therefore they are ignorant of him who is from above.

Finally Euclid among them flourishes especially in the disciplines of Geometry. But Aristotle and Theophrastus are held by them in admiration. And Galen by some of them is even adored. Who strive to assert the impiety of their heresy by those arts and doctrines; and by deceiving men ignorant of God they undermine the simplicity of the divine Scriptures and the sincerity of faith. But they do these things because they have not even become neighbors to the faith; therefore they also violate the divine Scriptures without any fear, and corrupting them say that they are emending them.
[Cap. 10 COMPLETE. CAPUT UNDECIMUM / On the distribution of sacred theology begins PHYS 323.]

source_text: 4. Naturalia cum supernaturalibus non sunt confundenda. Hinc S. Athanasius disp. 2. contra Arrianos: Quod de hominibus, inquit, id de Deo sentiendum non est. Confer dicta ad regulam primam. 5. A gubernatione civili ad administrationem spiritualem languida est illatio. Hinc Christus: Vos autem non sic, Luc. 22.v.26. confer Casaub. exerc. 14. disp. 5. & exerc. 18. d. 11. 12. IX. Secundo, Principium dependens est publicum aut privatum. X. Publicum est, quod universae Ecclesiae consensu consignatum est. XI. Estque socialis collationis aut fidelis relationis. XII. Socialis collatio fit vel in concilio sive synodo, aut simili aliquo consessu, cui praeest Spiritus S. judex in prophetarum Apostolorumque choro, lege scripta. Hoc colligitur ex Act. 15.v.28. Joh. 16.v.8.13. Joh. 5.v.45. 2. Regum 17.v.20. Gal. 6.v.16. Matth. 10.v.20. Vide D. Lutherum tom. 7. Jenens. t. Germ. de conciliis & ecclesia, & Jo. Calvinum lib. 4. instit. cap. 9. sect. 13. Guilielmum Whitakerum ad Duraeum lib. 4. de conciliis.
english: 4. Natural things are not to be confused with supernatural. Hence St. Athanasius, Disputation 2 against the Arians: What is said of men, he says, is not to be thought of God. Compare what was said at the first rule. 5. From civil government to spiritual administration the inference is weak. Hence Christ: But you not so ([[Luke 22:26 >> Bible:Luke 22:26]]); compare Casaubon, Exercitationes 14, disputation 5, and Exercitationes 18, chapters 11–12.

IX. Secondly, the dependent principle is public or private. X. Public is that which has been sealed by the consensus of the universal Church. XI. And it is of social collation or of faithful relation. XII. Social collation takes place either in a council or synod, or in some similar assembly, over which the Holy Spirit presides as judge in the choir of prophets and Apostles, by the written law. This is gathered from [[Acts 15:28 >> Bible:Acts 15:28]]; [[John 16:8 >> Bible:John 16:8]], [[John 16:13 >> Bible:John 16:13]]; [[John 5:45 >> Bible:John 5:45]]; [[2 Kings 17:20 >> Bible:2 Kings 17:20]]; [[Galatians 6:16 >> Bible:Galatians 6:16]]; [[Matthew 10:20 >> Bible:Matthew 10:20]]. See Luther, Jena German volume 7, On Councils and the Church; Calvin, Institutes book 4, chapter 9, section 13; William Whitaker against Duraeus, On Councils book 4.

source_text: Sophistae autem & falsi Theologi, qua tales, triplici fere probationum genere utuntur. Primum est pseudographikon, cum ad probandum theorema spirituale assumuntur quidem e sacris literis probationes, non tamen verae, vel ob perversam interpretationem, vel ob sinistram applicationem ad propositam quaestionem, qualia pseudographemata innumera occurrunt Arianorum & Photinianorum, ut & Paracelsistarum & Weigelianorum multorumque Jacob-Behmistarum & similium, qui multa scripturae testimonia ad absurdas & blasphemas opiniones detorquent, ut, cum oppugnant deitatem Filii & Spiritus sancti, veritatem naturae humanae ex Maria virgine assumptae, unionem personalem, & his connexa. Quod primum genus adversatur probationibus veris, Theologiae propriis, ac vernaculis, quia conficit syllogismum ex vernaculis quidem sumptionibus, non autem veris, ut philosophus loquitur lib. 1. Top. cap. 1. Alterum est sophisticum, quod opponitur dialecticis & communibus probationibus & committit aliquam vel in verbis conjunctis, vel in simplicibus, vel extra dictiones in rebus fallaciam. Tertium est interjectum inter duo priora, quod assumit principium quoddam heterogenes, alienum seu peregrinum, in suo quidem genere verum, sed ad aliud genus translatum inefficax ad id, quod est propositum. Hoc Aristoteles interdum vocat logikon, interdum vero absurdum & commentitium, ad propositam quaestionem coactum, lib. 13. metaphys. cap. 7. Hoc tertium vitiosae probationis genus nimis familiare fuit scholasticis, qui ad probanda theoremata spiritualia aptarunt principia philosophica, transeuntes ex alio genere in aliud contra leges analyticas, quae omnium terminorum syngeneian postulant. Hoc abutuntur Photiniani amathes kai ignari analyticorum, dum aeternam & hyperphysicam Filii Dei generationem physicis ratiunculis destruere conantur. Caeterum, ut analyticae probationes gignunt accuratam rerum cognitionem: ita pseudographai probationes efficiunt agnoian kai diathesin, ignorantiam pravae affectionis solida cognitioni contrariam. Sophisticae faciunt fucum & praestigiis quasi quibusdam ludificant. Heterogeneis peregrinae aliquam opinionem pro scientia afferunt. Hinc beatus Lutherus de Theologia Scholastica recte scribit, eam duntaxat esse opinionem, sive umbraticam & tenuem rerum spiritualium cognitionem, quia non e propriis, sed alienis sive diversi generis principiis spiritualia theoremata construit.
english: But sophists and false theologians, as such, use almost a threefold genus of proofs. The first is pseudographic — when for proving a spiritual theorem proofs are indeed assumed from the sacred letters, yet not true ones, either because of perverse interpretation or because of sinister application to the proposed question — of which pseudographemata countless occur among the Arians and Photinians, as also among Paracelsists and Weigelians and many Jacob-Boehmists and the like, who twist many Scripture testimonies to absurd and blasphemous opinions, as when they attack the deity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, the truth of the human nature assumed from the virgin Mary, the personal union, and things connected with these. This first genus is opposed to true proofs proper and vernacular to theology, because it constructs a syllogism from vernacular premises that are not true, as the philosopher speaks (Topics book 1, chapter 1).

The second is sophistic, which is opposed to dialectic and common proofs and commits some fallacy either in conjoined words, or in simple ones, or outside diction in things. The third is interposed between the two prior ones, which assumes some heterogeneous principle — alien or foreign — true indeed in its own genus, but transferred to another genus ineffective for what is proposed. Aristotle sometimes calls this logical, sometimes absurd and fictitious, forced toward the proposed question (Metaphysics book 13, chapter 7). This third genus of vicious proof was too familiar to the scholastics, who fitted philosophical principles to proving spiritual theorems, crossing from one genus into another against the analytic laws that demand kinship of all terms. The Photinians, unlearned and ignorant of analytics, abuse this when they try to destroy the eternal and hyperphysical generation of the Son of God with physical little reasonings.

Moreover, as analytic proofs beget accurate knowledge of things, so pseudographic proofs produce ignorance and a disposition — ignorance of a depraved affection contrary to solid cognition. Sophistic proofs make a show and as it were mock with certain juggling tricks. Heterogeneous foreign proofs bring forward some opinion for science. Hence blessed Luther rightly writes of Scholastic Theology that it is only opinion, or a shadowy and thin cognition of spiritual things, because it constructs spiritual theorems not from proper but from alien or diverse-genus principles.

source_text: Modus vero solvendi probationes pseudographicas non est unus. Nam interdum solvuntur adhibita sana principiorum interpretatione & monstrata sinistra applicatione ad propositam quaestionem: interdum per inficiationem vel etiam per oppositionem verorum principiorum e diversis scripturae locis inter se optime consentientium & ostensionem harmoniae & synapheias connexionis, quae verborum rerumque significatarum naturae convenienter veriorem sententiam confirmat & a sequiore destruitur & labefactatur: interdum aliqua limitatione & distinctione: interdum vero etiam per deductionem ad absurdum, quae negativo contradictionis principio nititur, plurimumque valet ad nervose labefactandas ejusmodi probationes & quicquid articulis fidei repugnat, ut videre est 1. Cor. 15. ubi Apostolus negantes resurrectionem mortuorum ad absurda quam plurima deducit. 2. Ubi deficit ratio, ibi incipit fidei aedificatio. Divina mysteria non rimanda, sed miranda. Hinc S. Athanasius ad Serapionem: Dei, ait, cognitio fide comprehendenda, non ratione humana exquirenda. Fides praesit, ratio subsit.
english: But the mode of solving pseudographic proofs is not one. For sometimes they are solved by applying a sound interpretation of the principles and showing the sinister application to the proposed question; sometimes by denial or even by opposing true principles from diverse Scripture places that agree best among themselves, and by showing the harmony and connection which, agreeably to the nature of the words and things signified, confirms the truer sentence and is destroyed and weakened by the weaker; sometimes by some limitation and distinction; sometimes even by deduction to absurdity, which rests on the negative principle of contradiction and has the greatest force for vigorously weakening such proofs and whatever conflicts with the articles of faith — as may be seen in [[1 Corinthians 15 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15]], where the Apostle leads those denying the resurrection of the dead to as many absurdities as possible.

2. Where reason fails, there faith's edifice begins. Divine mysteries are not to be pried into, but to be wondered at. Hence St. Athanasius to Serapion: The knowledge of God, he says, is to be comprehended by faith, not sought out by human reason. Let faith preside; let reason sit under.

source_text: XV. Sunt autem hic quoque notandae regulae. 1. Inter testimonium phrasesque scripturae & inter testimonium phrasesque Ecclesiae accurate & caute distinguendum est; ut, panis, quem frangimus, est communio corporis Christi 1. Cor. 10.v.16. Panis est corpus Christi. Illa scripturae, haec Ecclesiae phrasis est. Utraque vera quidem: illa tamen propria, haec impropria est. 2. In publico testimonio, quamvis una sit eademque veritas, non tamen semper una eademque est authoritas. Major enim est symboli Apostolici authoritas, minor vero confessionis Augustanae, Gallicae, Helveticae, Belgicae, Anglicanae & similium. 3. Publicum testimonium, caeteris paribus, privato merito est anteponendum. Sic, totius Ecclesiae confessio antecellit confessioni unius alicujus doctoris; etiamsi tam illic, quam hic una veritas. 4. Testimoniorum, quae a patribus sumuntur unica norma & fidius lapis est sacra scriptura. Sic Augustinus lib. de unitate Ecclesiae cap. 5. Non, inquit, audiendum in Ecclesia: haec dico, haec dicis: sed haec dicit DOMINUS. Digna quoque observatu hic est monela Nicephori Gregorae lib. X. historiae Romanae sive Byzantinae pag. 235. Caeterum, ait, illud quoque scire est opera pretium, non simpliciter, nec uno modo sanctorum patrum scripturas intelligendas esse. Quarum aliae didaskalikos kai parainetikos blepousi, ad docendum & monendum accommodate sunt personarum & temporum habita ratione, sed religiose omnia. Nam aliae dogmatikos, decreta continent, aliae enkomiastikos, laudationes, aliae agonistikos, disceptationes. Neque vero disceptationes Veterum alio transferendae sunt. Neque enim, si quis pugnans cum hostibus, & toto animo in gladium & clypeum intentus, commilitonem ante pedes stantem prostraverit, vel lex ea putanda est, vel is accusandus qui id fecit, cogitationem a lucta trabente necessitate, eo minime sinente ut id quod factum est, aliter fieret. Ergo neque hoc sic agendum est, neque laudationibus vice legum utendum. Ars enim laudantibus quidvis dicendi licentiam dedit. Quae vero dogmata sanxerunt & promulgarunt, in iis demum rectum & tutum est veluti canonibus & amussi religionis uti. Haec Nicephorus, quae tamen ex regula nostra ad lydium scripturae semper exigenda sunt, ut supra demonstratum est.
english: XV. And here too rules are to be noted. 1. Between the testimony and phrases of Scripture and between the testimony and phrases of the Church one must accurately and carefully distinguish — as: the bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ ([[1 Corinthians 10:16 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 10:16]]); and the bread is the body of Christ. The former is Scripture's phrase, the latter the Church's. Both indeed true: yet the former proper, the latter improper.

2. In public testimony, although there is one and the same truth, yet there is not always one and the same authority. For greater is the authority of the Apostolic Symbol, but lesser that of the Augsburg, Gallican, Helvetic, Belgian, Anglican confession and the like. 3. Public testimony, other things equal, is deservedly to be preferred to private. Thus the confession of the whole Church surpasses the confession of some one doctor — even if there as here there is one truth.

4. Of testimonies taken from the fathers the unique norm and touchstone is Sacred Scripture. Thus Augustine, On the Unity of the Church chapter 5: It is not to be heard in the Church, he says: I say this, you say this — but the LORD says this. Worthy of observation here too is the warning of Nicephorus Gregoras, Roman or Byzantine History book 10, page 235: Moreover, he says, it is also worth knowing that the writings of the holy fathers are not to be understood simply nor in one way. Of which some look to teaching and admonishing — are accommodated to teaching and admonishing, persons and times being considered, yet all religiously. For some contain decrees dogmatically; others praises encomiastically; others disputations combatively. Nor indeed are the ancients' disputations to be transferred elsewhere. For if someone fighting with enemies, and with whole mind intent on sword and shield, should strike down a fellow-soldier standing before his feet, neither is that to be thought a law, nor is he to be accused who did it, necessity drawing the thought from the struggle, by no means allowing that what was done should happen otherwise. Therefore neither is this to be so done, nor are praises to be used in place of laws. For art has given to those praising license to say anything. But those dogmas which they sanctioned and promulgated — in those alone it is right and safe to use them as canons and the plumbline of religion. Thus Nicephorus — which yet by our rule are always to be tested against Scripture's Lydian stone, as was demonstrated above.

source_text: Hic tamen nota, cum propria & interior mysteriorum, quae in controversiam adducta sunt, veritas Dei verbo explicanda venit, canon secundum humanae rationis naturalem modulum & hactenus a philosophis descriptam, nullo modo, sed secundum ingenium & dictamen fidei, quae sub nova luce rationem in mysteriis suis verbo Dei subjicit, etiam contra caecae rationis caecum judicium, formanda est. Verbi gratia, scriptura docet, Mariae unigenitum esse Dei filium unigenitum, & hunc hominem, qui e Maria genitus est, esse aeternum Deum, item, Deum esse passum, & his similia. Quae verba significatione sua nativa non pariunt eum sensum, cujus ratio per lumen suum naturale capax sit, quique secundum illius normam in praedicationum logicarum generibus delineatam, mensurari capique possit. Neque hic opus est, ut horum verborum significationes tam diu artificiosis translationibus vertantur, dum ejusmodi sensum pariant, qui naturali captu rationis, secundum regulas logicas, comprehendi possit: quia veritas mysteriorum & institutorum divinorum naturalem rationis humanae captum excedit, neque humanae sapientiae, logicisque regulis sese attemperat, sicuti res & actiones rationi subjectae, secundum regulas logicas disponi atque tractari solent. Logica enim est instar regulae Lesbiae, quae sese rebus accommodare debet, ut sunt: neque res rerumque connexiones necessariae & contingentes, natura notae aut divinitus revelatae, torqueri ad regulas a Logicis ex consideratione rerum naturalium & moralium repertas. Ubi igitur veritas enunciati in scripturis revelatur singularis & inusitata, ibi logicus cessat, Deo revelanti, si Christianus est, credit & regulas suas deficere lubens fatetur, propriaque decreta in illius honorem cordate rescindit. Quicquid vero ratio recta demonstrat alienum esse a sapientia, bonitate, aequitate & justitia Dei, usqueadeo ut etiam ab humana alienum sit, id de plano rejiciendum & respuendum est. Imo quicquid absurdum, falsum & stultum est secundum rectam rationem, id apud Deum & ubique absurdum, falsum & stultum est, ut, siquis dicat, unum esse duo, unum & duo non facere tria, tria esse paria, quatuor imparia, & ab aequalibus aequalia demamus, quae relinquuntur, non esse aequalia, & si quid aliud contradictionem revera implicat. Fieri enim nequit, ut duo contradictoria sint simul vera. Fides adsit, & nulla erit quaestio. Nam mysteria scrutari, est temeritas: credere pietas; nosse, aeterna beatitas. Est vero & hic grave offendiculum, quomodo fides Christiana praevaleat scientiae philosophicae? Durandus: Omni, inquit, scienti potest constare de conclusione sua, quod sit vera, & quod impossibile sit aliter se habere. Sed de conclusione deducta ex principiis tantum creditis, non potest constare deducenti, quod impossibile sit, eam aliter se habere, neque quod sit vera. Non enim plus constare potest de conclusione, quam de principiis, cum notitia conclusionum dependeat ex notitia principiorum. Sed respondemus, verbum Dei esse quidem firmissimum fidei principium, sed quod sua habet tekmeria, quae sacra Biblia arguant esse verissimi Dei verum verbum, & quamvis in his ipsis subinde nutet mens humana humano modo agens, tamen Deus eam per id ipsum verbum illuminando & voluntatem in obsequium trahendo, ita firmat certitudinem principii, ut fidelis laeto pectore illud sanguine suo obsignare non dubitet. Principio sic stabilito & immoto, quicquid in eo comprehenditur, pari firmitate creditur, ut sic & principii & conclusionum inde depromptarum infallibilis detur plerophoria. Si enim ita procedatur, ut tekmerion deductioni, qua persuasus homo initio credat, verbum propheticum & Apostolicum, esse verissimi Dei verissimum verbum, conjungatur verbi illius potentia & efficacia, in illuminatione mentis & corroboratione assensus auditoris, perpetuo pendentis a verbo, tum quod alias perpetuo fluctuat, in animis nostris firmissimum sistitur. Et hinc dependet conclusio Richardi de S. Victore, Doctoris solidi dicti: Quotquot veraciter fideles sumus, id est, vera fide, per illuminationem divinam, mediante verbo Dei accensam, donati sumus, nihil certius, nihil constantius tenemus, quam quod fide apprehendimus. Utinam attenderent Judaei, utinam animadverterent pagani, cum quanta conscientiae securitate, ad divinum judicium poterimus accedere. Nonne cum omni fiducia, Deo dicere poterimus: Domine, si error est, a te ipso sumus decepti? Nam ista in nobis, tantis signis & prodigiis confirmata sunt & talibus, quae nonnisi per te fieri possunt, quae & a viris summae sanctitatis nobis sunt tradita, cum summa atque authentica attestatione probata, teipso cooperante sermonem confirmante subsequentibus signis? Notetur hic cooperatio Domini, cum verbo Dei praedicato, praeter externa miracula, sicut Christus Joh. 5.v.20. vivificationem, quam per euangelium praestat, inter opera visibilibus signis majora refert.
english: Note here, however: when the proper and interior truth of the mysteries brought into controversy comes to be explained by God's Word, the canon is by no means to be formed according to the natural measure of human reason and that hitherto described by the philosophers, but according to the genius and dictate of faith, which under a new light subjects reason in its mysteries to God's Word, even against blind reason's blind judgment. For example, Scripture teaches that Mary's only-begotten is God's only-begotten Son, and that this man begotten from Mary is the eternal God; likewise, that God suffered, and things like these. Which words by their native signification do not yield that sense of which reason by its natural light is capable, and which can be measured and grasped according to that norm delineated in the genera of logical predications.

Nor is it needful here that the significations of these words be turned so long by artful translations until they yield such a sense as can be comprehended by reason's natural capacity according to logical rules — because the truth of the divine mysteries and institutions exceeds the natural capacity of human reason, and does not temper itself to human wisdom and logical rules, as things and actions subject to reason are customarily disposed and treated according to logical rules. For logic is like the Lesbian rule, which ought to accommodate itself to things as they are; nor are things and their necessary and contingent connections, known by nature or divinely revealed, to be twisted to rules found by logicians from considering natural and moral things. Where therefore the truth of a statement is revealed in the Scriptures as singular and unusual, there the logician ceases; if he is a Christian he believes God revealing, and gladly confesses that his rules fail, and heartily rescinds his own decrees in God's honor.

But whatever right reason demonstrates to be alien to God's wisdom, goodness, equity, and justice — so far that it is alien even from the human — that is to be flatly rejected and spat out. Indeed whatever is absurd, false, and foolish according to right reason is absurd, false, and foolish before God and everywhere — as if someone should say that one is two, that one and two do not make three, that three are even, four odd, and that if we take equals from equals what remain are not equal, and if anything else truly implies a contradiction. For it cannot be that two contradictories are true at once. Let faith be present, and there will be no question. For to scrutinize mysteries is rashness; to believe is piety; to know is eternal blessedness.

Yet here too there is a grave stumbling-block: how does Christian faith prevail over philosophical science? Durandus says: To every knower it can be established concerning his conclusion that it is true, and that it is impossible for it to be otherwise. But concerning a conclusion deduced from principles only believed, it cannot be established for the one deducing that it is impossible for it to be otherwise, nor that it is true. For no more can be established concerning the conclusion than concerning the principles, since knowledge of conclusions depends on knowledge of principles. But we reply that God's Word is indeed the firmest principle of faith, yet one that has its own tokens which argue that the sacred Bibles are the true Word of the most true God; and although in these themselves the human mind acting in a human way now and then wavers, yet God, by illuminating it through that very Word and drawing the will into obedience, so confirms the certainty of the principle that the believer with joyful breast does not hesitate to seal it with his blood. With the principle thus established and unmoved, whatever is comprehended in it is believed with equal firmness, so that thus an infallible full assurance of both the principle and the conclusions drawn from it is given.

For if one proceeds so that to the deduction of tokens by which a persuaded man at first believes that the prophetic and Apostolic Word is the most true Word of the most true God, there is joined that Word's power and efficacy in illuminating the mind and strengthening the hearer's assent perpetually depending on the Word — then what otherwise perpetually fluctuates is set most firmly in our souls. And on this depends the conclusion of Richard of St. Victor, called a solid Doctor: As many of us as are truly faithful — that is, gifted with true faith kindled by divine illumination through the mediation of God's Word — hold nothing more certain, nothing more constant, than what we apprehend by faith. Would that the Jews would attend, would that the pagans would notice, with how great security of conscience we shall be able to approach the divine judgment. Shall we not with all confidence be able to say to God: Lord, if it is error, we have been deceived by you yourself? For these things in us have been confirmed by such great signs and wonders and such as can be done only through you, which also have been handed down to us by men of highest holiness, proved with highest and authentic attestation, you yourself cooperating, confirming the word with following signs? Note here the Lord's cooperation with God's preached Word, besides external miracles — as Christ ([[John 5:20 >> Bible:John 5:20]]) reckons the vivification which he performs through the gospel among works greater than visible signs.

source_text: Quod enim in aliis etiam disciplinis fieri consuevit, ut interdum dialectici syllogismi praemittantur analyticis, interdum vero postponantur pro varietate controversiarum: idem quoque nihil vetat fieri in sacra Theologia, in qua, ut dixi, duo sunt legitimarum probationum genera, perinde ut in aliis quoque disciplinis. Prius continet probationes analyticas, didascalicas, quae & mere spirituales & Theologicae, idiai, vernaculae, itemque pneumatos & dynameos Theou, spirituales & efficaces demonstrationes cum Apostolo dici queunt. Posterius vero habet probationes communes & dialecticas, quas triplices jam paucis indicavimus. Analyticae vero, quae mere spirituales sunt, aut ducuntur e verbo Dei scripto & divinitus revelato, vel tradito a Christo e sinu Patris, a prophetis, per quos spiritus Domini locutus est, & Apostolis, quorum auctoritati, cum certam habuerint non tantum in specie, sed & in individuis promissionem spiritus sancti, nulla auctoritas humana vel synodorum, vel etiam patrum, tam Latinorum, quam Graecorum aequanda est, nisi cum scriptura loquantur: aut ducuntur e propria rerum spiritualium natura, de quibus agitur, quae & ipsa e scripturis colligitur beneficio analyticae doctrinae. Priores probationes ad articulos fidei probandos, omnium sunt efficacissimae, potentissimae. Deus enim auctor & fons rerum omnium, & ipsa veritas est. Ex Platone lib. 2. de rep. in altera formula constituenda religionis: Deus, ait, est simplex, & verax & opere & verbis, neque mutatur ipse, neque alios decipit, neque simulacrorum objectis, neque sermonibus, neque signis immissis, neque per vigilias, neque in somno. Ad veritatem Dei in verbo accedit omnipotentia, ad quos duos fontes certitudinis Servator noster in confutatione Sadducaeorum respexit Matth. 22.v.29. Posteriores vero etiam probationes analyticae maximam habent vim ad comparandum solidam rerum spiritualium scientiam, quia & ipsae e salutaribus Israelis fontibus hauriuntur, ut, quando de peccato originis, de fide, de justificatione, deque caeteris rebus spiritualibus agitur, e propria earum natura probationes petuntur: sed plus habent artis, artificiosaeque industriae. Ut, si quis velit dictum Paulinum probare analytice: Justificatos fide habere pacatam conscientiam. Quia oportet primo omnium praecognoscere quid sit justificatio, quid fides, quid pax, quid conscientia, quod sine analytica doctrina sacris literis applicata difficulter fieri potest. Constitutis vero horum extremorum conclusionis definitionibus partim perfectis, partim etiam onomatodesi, nominalibus, facile fit probatio analytica. Quicunque enim nititur fiducia misericordiae divinae propter Christi meritum, pacatam habet conscientiam. Atqui justificatus fide nititur fiducia misericordiae Dei propter meritum Christi. Ergo justificatus fide habet pacatam conscientiam. Caeterae omnes probationes, quarum legitimus usus est in theologia nostra, tantum sunt dialecticae, de quibus paulo ante diximus, una cum earum usu. Etsi vero universa topica plurimum momenti habeant in studio theologico; cum primis tamen discenda sunt e quatuor progymnasmatis sub finem primi Topicorum expositis praecepta distinguendi ea, quae multis modis dicuntur, item inveniendi differentias, & perspiciendi similitudines rerum: quia nisi distinguantur ambigua, ut vox justitiae, Euangelii, fidei & similes, & ea, quae similia sunt, certis differentiis inventis separentur, ut lex & euangelium, justitia activa & passiva, justificatio & regeneratio, fides & bona opera, charitas, fides & spes, variis logomachiais verborum pugnis & periculosis disputationibus, quas Paulus vitare passim jubet, desumanae portae aperiuntur. Huc quoque pertinent liber 6. & 7. Topicorum, quorum praeceptis examinantur ab aliis constitutae definitiones, ut, an euangelium sit concio poenitentiae: & fontes similitudinesque differentiarum ostenduntur. E quibus patet, non allotrion, alienum a nostra religione & sacris literis duplicem res spirituales tractandi modum, acroamaticum seu analyticum & exotericum seu dialecticum, sed potius esse; solidum autem & falsi Theologi, qua tales, tractationibus theologicis convenientissimum.
english: For what is also customary in other disciplines — that sometimes dialectic syllogisms are premised to analytic ones, sometimes postponed according to the variety of controversies — nothing forbids the same in sacred theology, in which, as I said, there are two genera of legitimate proofs, just as in other disciplines too. The former contains analytic, didactic proofs, which can also be called with the Apostle merely spiritual and theological, proper, vernacular, and likewise of the Spirit and power of God — spiritual and effective demonstrations. The latter has common and dialectic proofs, which we have already briefly indicated as threefold.

But analytic proofs, which are merely spiritual, are either drawn from the written and divinely revealed Word of God — or handed down by Christ from the Father's bosom, by the prophets through whom the Lord's Spirit spoke, and by the Apostles, to whose authority, since they had a certain promise of the Holy Spirit not only in kind but also in individuals, no human authority of synods or even of fathers, Latin or Greek, is to be equated unless they speak with Scripture — or they are drawn from the proper nature of the spiritual things under discussion, which itself is gathered from the Scriptures by the benefit of analytic doctrine. The former proofs for proving the articles of faith are of all the most effective and powerful. For God is the author and fountain of all things, and truth itself. From Plato, Republic book 2, in the second formula for constituting religion: God, he says, is simple and truthful in work and words; he neither changes himself nor deceives others — neither by objects of images, nor by speeches, nor by signs sent in, nor through waking, nor in sleep. To God's truth in the Word is added omnipotence — to which two springs of certainty our Savior looked in confuting the Sadducees ([[Matthew 22:29 >> Bible:Matthew 22:29]]).

But the later analytic proofs also have the greatest force for acquiring solid science of spiritual things, because they too are drawn from Israel's saving springs — as when one treats of original sin, faith, justification, and other spiritual things, proofs are sought from their proper nature; but they have more of art and skillful industry. For example, if someone wishes to prove analytically the Pauline saying: That those justified by faith have a pacified conscience. For one must first of all know beforehand what justification is, what faith, what peace, what conscience — which can hardly be done without analytic doctrine applied to the sacred letters. But once definitions of these extremes of the conclusion are constituted, partly perfect, partly also nominal, analytic proof becomes easy: Whoever rests on trust in divine mercy for Christ's merit has a pacified conscience. But the one justified by faith rests on trust in God's mercy for Christ's merit. Therefore the one justified by faith has a pacified conscience.

All the other proofs whose legitimate use is in our theology are only dialectic, of which we spoke a little earlier, together with their use. And although the whole of topics has much weight in theological study, yet first of all there are to be learned from the four progymnasmata set out at the end of the first book of the Topics the precepts of distinguishing things said in many ways, of finding differences, and of discerning likenesses of things — because unless ambiguities are distinguished (as the word justice, Gospel, faith, and the like) and things that are alike are separated by certain differences found (as law and gospel, active and passive righteousness, justification and regeneration, faith and good works, charity, faith and hope), doors are opened to various word-fights and dangerous disputations which Paul everywhere bids us avoid. Here also pertain Topics books 6 and 7, by whose precepts definitions constituted by others are examined — for example, whether the gospel is a sermon of repentance — and the springs and likenesses of differences are shown. From which it is clear that a double mode of treating spiritual things — acroamatic or analytic, and exoteric or dialectic — is not alien to our religion and the sacred letters, but rather is proper; and that it is most fitting for the solid — and to expose the false — theologian as such in theological treatments.

source_text: Quod ideo addo, quia, jactis solidis & firmis fundamentis, aut etiam cum erudiendi sunt prorsus imperiti, Christus ipse & Apostoli dialecticas quoque adhibent probationes & oratorias artes, ut videre est apud Andream Hyperium Flandrum, olim professorem Marpurgensem, in Topicis Theologicis, qualia sunt 1. loca topica, communia pluribus disciplinis. 2. probationes, quae petuntur a decretis & judiciis conciliorum, a consuetudine Ecclesiae, ab humanis traditionibus, ab opinionibus & sententiis patrum tam Latinorum, quam Graecorum. Horum enim omnium autoritas tantum est probabilis, & nititur autoritate canonicae scripturae, id quod protestantes uno ore testantur & Bellarminus quoque alicubi haud diffitetur. 3. Probationes, quae petuntur non e propria, sed communi rerum spiritualium natura, de quibus agitur, quae kat analogian tantum dialecticae & logicae dicuntur, etiamsi earum termini mere sint spirituales. Usurpantur autem duabus potissimum de causis. 1. Propter auditores ignaros mysteriorum divinorum, imperitosque linguae scripturae. Sic Paulus in Actis utitur auctoritate Arati ad coarguendos Stoicos & Epicureos, qui scripturas non admisissent, sicuti neque hodie Mahomedani: item Epimenidis poetae contra Cretenses; & Menandri ad corrigendos Corinthios. Sic Christus in erudiendo populo, ut plurimum utitur argumentis communibus & dialecticis a similibus & id genus aliis, tum temporis in Syria usitatis. Est hoc utile eis paideusin. Acroamatice vero Christus docet discipulos suos & analytice disputat contra pharisaeos, Sadducaeos, Satanam. 2. Propter illustrationem eorum, quae acroamatice sive analytice prius demonstrata sunt.
english: I add this because, when solid and firm foundations have been laid, or even when the wholly uninstructed are to be taught, Christ himself and the Apostles also employ dialectic proofs and oratorical arts — as may be seen in Andreas Hyperius of Flanders, formerly professor at Marburg, in his Theological Topics — such as: (1) topical places common to several disciplines; (2) proofs sought from the decrees and judgments of councils, from the Church's custom, from human traditions, from the opinions and sentences of the Latin as well as the Greek fathers — for the authority of all these is only probable, and rests on the authority of canonical Scripture, which the Protestants with one mouth testify and Bellarmine also somewhere does not deny; (3) proofs sought not from the proper but from the common nature of the spiritual things under discussion, which are called dialectic and logical only by analogy, even if their terms are merely spiritual.

And they are used chiefly for two causes. (1) For hearers ignorant of the divine mysteries and unskilled in Scripture's language. Thus Paul in Acts uses the authority of Aratus to refute the Stoics and Epicureans, who would not have admitted the Scriptures, just as Mohammedans do not today; likewise the poet Epimenides against the Cretans; and Menander to correct the Corinthians. Thus Christ, in teaching the people, for the most part uses common and dialectic arguments from likes and other such things customary then in Syria. This is useful for instruction. But acroamatically Christ teaches his disciples and analytically disputes against the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Satan. (2) For illustrating those things which were first demonstrated acroamatically or analytically.

source_text: 5. Quaedam in sacra scriptura sunt & dicuntur: quaedam in ea sunt, etsi non dicuntur. Hinc Nazianzenus lib. 5. Theologiae. Nam, inquit, in scriptura ponuntur quaedam quod ad verba & sensum simul: quaedam quod ad sensum tantum. 6. Mutua collatio attendat aliqua in scriptura contineri explicite: nonnulla vero duntaxat implicite. 7. Testificatio est duplex, dogmatica, quae fit de fidei nostrae capitibus; & historica, quae fit de divinis libris. 8. Etiamsi haeresis aliqua in publico concilio non sit damnata: Ea tamen ex verbo Dei debet dijudicari atque refutari, juxta illud 1. Joh. 4.v.1. Hinc Athanasius epistola de Synodo Ariminensi, Frustra, inquit, circumcursantes praetexunt, se ob fidem synodos postulare, cum sit divina scriptura omnibus potentior. 9. Doctorum post Apostolorum aetatem conclusiones ne temere abeant in normas fidei, studiose caveto. Docet enim Apostolus 1. Cor. 2.v.4. saepius quod sermo & praedicatio mea non in persuasibilibus humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in demonstratione spiritus & potentiae sive virtutis, h.e. confirmatus, 1. testimoniis jam olim a spiritu & potentia Dei prolatis, 2. Pet. 1.v.20.21. 2. peculiariter tunc etiam visibili Spiritus sancti effusione, & variis potentiae divinae miraculis: quae omnia opponit demonstrationibus philosophiae humanae. 3. affectu charitatis & robore patientiae, a quibus oriebatur sermo; cum quibus dicebatur; & ad quae potenter efficienda unice tendebat: quae opponit affectatae eloquentiae & suadae humanae. Confer 1. Cor. 4.v.19. 1. Joh. 3.v.4.24. & 4.v.7. Col. 1. 1. Tim. 1.v.5. Ille igitur verba sua ex scripturis probans, additis evidenter talibus signis, talibusque affectibus; ac spiritualia spiritualibus ita aptans, ut 1. & praesentia Dei, de qua loquebatur, & sermo, quo loquebatur, spiritualis potius ac potens esset, quam speciosus foris ad sensum saeculi: 2. conclusio probata & testimonium probans eandem spiraret vim: conclusiones porro tales ex principiis deduxit, quae & ipsae nobis sint principia. At nos neque signis talibus, neque simili affectu dicentes, contenti necessario principiis in scriptura positis, conclusiones colligimus in tantum firmas, in quantum collata principiis dictis, eis conformes esse, & ex eis fluere evidens factum fuerit. 10. Consequentiae dubiae, obscurae, difficiles, aut falsae ne vertantur in axiomata omni exceptione majora, neque omnes controversiae in necessaria dogmata. 11. Etsi non plane proscribi debeant notiones secundae ob alterum legitimarum probationum communium & dialecticarum genus: tamen verus & sobrius usus organi & perfectio judicii logici etiam in controversiis theologicis magis consistit in distinctione probationum analyticarum & dialecticarum, quibus & affines sunt rhetoricae, quam in abusu utriusque oppositarum apateticarum, pseudographikon, sophisticarum & heterogeneorum. Cum enim mysteria pleraque omnia, & res quaedam spirituales & divinae, voces generis, speciei, differentiae, accidentis, subjecti, formae, & aliarum similium secundarum notionum plane respuant, si iis uti velis in ejusmodi mysteriis tantum analogice contra haereticos, facile fieri potest, ut eis aperias kataphyges latibula, quibus errores suos occultent.
english: 5. Certain things in Sacred Scripture are and are said; certain things are in it, even if they are not said. Hence Nazianzen, Theology book 5: For, he says, in Scripture some things are set down as to words and sense together; some as to sense only. 6. Mutual collation should attend that some things are contained in Scripture explicitly; but some only implicitly. 7. Testification is twofold — dogmatic, which is made concerning the heads of our faith; and historical, which is made concerning the divine books.

8. Even if some heresy has not been condemned in a public council: yet it ought to be judged and refuted from God's Word, according to that of [[1 John 4:1 >> Bible:1 John 4:1]]. Hence Athanasius, letter on the Synod of Ariminum: In vain, he says, those running about pretend that they demand synods for the faith, since divine Scripture is more powerful than all. 9. Carefully beware lest the conclusions of doctors after the Apostles' age rashly pass into norms of faith. For the Apostle teaches ([[1 Corinthians 2:4 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:4]]) often that my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power or virtue — that is, confirmed (1) by testimonies already long ago brought forth by the Spirit and power of God ([[2 Peter 1:20 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:20]]-[[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]); (2) peculiarly then also by the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and by various miracles of divine power — all of which he opposes to the demonstrations of human philosophy; (3) by the affection of charity and the strength of patience, from which the speech arose, with which it was spoken, and to effecting which powerfully it uniquely tended — which he opposes to affected eloquence and human persuasion. Compare [[1 Corinthians 4:19 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 4:19]]; [[1 John 3:4 >> Bible:1 John 3:4]], [[1 John 3:24 >> Bible:1 John 3:24]]; [[1 John 4:7 >> Bible:1 John 4:7]]; Colossians 1; [[1 Timothy 1:5 >> Bible:1 Timothy 1:5]].

He therefore, proving his words from the Scriptures, with such signs and such affections evidently added, and so fitting spiritual things to spiritual that (1) both God's presence of which he spoke, and the speech by which he spoke, was rather spiritual and powerful than outwardly specious to the age's sense; (2) the proved conclusion and the proving testimony breathed the same force — further deduced such conclusions from principles as are themselves principles for us. But we, speaking neither with such signs nor with like affection, content with the principles necessarily set in Scripture, gather conclusions firm only insofar as, compared with the said principles, it has been made evident that they conform to them and flow from them.

10. Doubtful, obscure, difficult, or false consequences are not to be turned into axioms beyond all exception, nor all controversies into necessary dogmas. 11. Although second notions ought not to be plainly proscribed on account of the other genus of legitimate common and dialectic proofs: yet the true and sober use of the organon and the perfection of logical judgment even in theological controversies consists more in distinguishing analytic and dialectic proofs — to which rhetorical ones are also akin — than in abusing either of the opposed deceptive, pseudographic, sophistic, and heterogeneous proofs. For since most mysteries, and certain spiritual and divine things, plainly reject the voices of genus, species, difference, accident, subject, form, and other like second notions — if you wish to use them in such mysteries only analogically against heretics, it can easily happen that you open them hiding-places of refuge in which to conceal their errors.

source_text: XVI. Extra ecclesiam est testimonium philosophorum, poetarum, historicorum, legislatorumque gentilium, Mercurii Trismegisti & Sibyllarum, quo veritas & aequitas Christianae fidei a patribus nonnunquam asseritur. Hoc testimonio, tanquam argumento ad hominem, non vero ut fidem & doctrinam caelitus revelatam humanis testimoniis firmarem, usus aliquando non erubuit Apostolus Paulus Act. 17.v.23.24.28. 1. Cor. 15.v.33. Tit. 1.v.12. Hoc non raro usi sunt doctissimi patres, Clemens Alexandrinus, Justinus Martyr, Tertullianus, Gregorius Nazianzenus, Lactantius, Augustinus & alii, quibus cum atheis & gentilibus potissimum negotium fuit. De Mercurio & Sibyllinis oraculis, quae hodieque leguntur, viro summo, Isaaco Casaubono exerc. 1. ad apparat. annal. Num. XVIII. & XIX. lubens adstipulor, de quibus negari non potest, in illis capita religionis non pauca, puta, de uno Deo, de sacrosancta Trinitate, de verbo Filio Dei, per quem mundus fuit conditus, de nascituro Christo ex virgine, de passione ipsius & cruce, de regeneratione per baptismum in vitam aeternam, de futuro judicio, & item alia, sic clare & perspicuis verbis inveniri exposita, ut vix ac ne vix quidem simile quid e tota lege Mosis & prophetis possit afferri. Sed vir eximius ingenue profitetur omnia hujus generis sive hujus Mercurii, sive Sibyllarum oracula ante nuntiata, quo apertiora sunt, eo sibi fieri suspectiora, eaque supposititia candidis redargutionibus demonstrat, 1. quia mysteria Christiana ante Christum fuerunt abscondita, Col. 1.v.26. Rom. 16.v.25. Eph. 3.v.9. quae tamen planissime explicantur in libro Mercurii & Sibyllinis carminibus, quae vel JESUM CHRISTUM acrostichide, sine ambagibus aut aenigmatis, ipso etiam nomine indicant, factaque ipsius narrant. Nam verbo Dei contrarium videtur existimare, tam profunda mysteria gentibus fuisse clarius proposita, quam populo Dei, quem Deus prophetarum voce ita erudivit, ut per obscuros rerum futurarum typos ad Christum, tanquam manu paedagogi deduxerit, Gal. 3.v.24. 2. quia veteres Graeci, Plato, Aristoteles, Theophrastus & tot alii curiosissimi omnium disciplinarum scrutatores, eorum, quae hodie in Mercurio isto & Sibyllis miramur, nullum prorsus vestigium ostendunt. 3. quia solemne fuit primis ecclesiae temporibus bono fine falsos libros fingere, quo facilius nova doctrina a gentium sapientibus admitteretur: quorum plurimos enumerat & jure optimo damnat Gelasius papa decreto suo & Romani concilii. Et in hunc censum referenda sunt oracula illa Sibyllina, quae arcana religionis nostrae apertius explicant, quam factum sit unquam a Dei prophetis: item liber integer, qui sub nomine Mercurii Trismegisti circumferri ab aliquot seculis coepit, pseudepigraphos falso inscriptus, quippe qui Christiani alicujus vel potius semichristiani merum figmentum est, ut Casaubonus noster ex re & dictione multis solide demonstrat. 4. quia ejusmodi scripta quam primum prodierе plurimis fuere suspecta. Nam verissime b. Augustinus lib. 18. de C.D. cap. 47. Quaecunque aliorum prophetiae de Dei per Christum Jesum gratia proferuntur, possunt putari a Christianis esse confictae. Ideo nihil est firmius ad convincendum quoslibet alienos, si de hac re contenderint, nostrosque fulciendos, si recte sapuerint, quam ut divina praedicta de Christo ea proferantur, quae in Judaeorum scripta sunt codicibus.
english: XVI. Outside the Church is the testimony of gentile philosophers, poets, historians, and legislators, of Mercury Trismegistus and the Sibyls, by which the truth and equity of the Christian faith is sometimes asserted by the fathers. By this testimony, as an argument ad hominem — not truly that I might confirm faith and doctrine revealed from heaven by human testimonies — the Apostle Paul sometimes did not blush to use ([[Acts 17:23 >> Bible:Acts 17:23]]-[[Acts 17:24 >> Bible:Acts 17:24]], [[Acts 17:28 >> Bible:Acts 17:28]]; [[1 Corinthians 15:33 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:33]]; [[Titus 1:12 >> Bible:Titus 1:12]]). This the most learned fathers have not rarely used — Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, Tertullian, Gregory Nazianzen, Lactantius, Augustine, and others — whose business was chiefly with atheists and gentiles.

Concerning Mercury and the Sibylline oracles which are still read today, I gladly assent to that highest man Isaac Casaubon (Exercitationes 1 to the Apparatus of the Annals, Numbers XVIII and XIX), concerning which it cannot be denied that in them not a few heads of religion — for example, concerning one God, the most holy Trinity, the Word the Son of God through whom the world was made, Christ to be born of a virgin, his passion and cross, regeneration through baptism into eternal life, the future judgment, and likewise other things — are found so clearly and in perspicuous words set forth that scarcely, indeed scarcely at all, anything similar can be brought from the whole law of Moses and the prophets. But the excellent man frankly professes that all oracles of this kind, whether of this Mercury or of the Sibyls announced beforehand, the more open they are, the more suspect they become to him; and he demonstrates them to be spurious by candid refutations: (1) because Christian mysteries were hidden before Christ ([[Colossians 1:26 >> Bible:Colossians 1:26]]; [[Romans 16:25 >> Bible:Romans 16:25]]; [[Ephesians 3:9 >> Bible:Ephesians 3:9]]), which yet are most plainly explained in Mercury's book and the Sibylline songs, which even indicate JESUS CHRIST by acrostic, without circumlocutions or enigmas, by the very name, and narrate his deeds. For it seems contrary to God's Word to think that such deep mysteries were proposed more clearly to the gentiles than to God's people, whom God so instructed by the prophets' voice that through obscure types of future things he led them to Christ as by a pedagogue's hand ([[Galatians 3:24 >> Bible:Galatians 3:24]]).

(2) Because the ancient Greeks — Plato, Aristotle, Theophrastus, and so many other most curious scrutinizers of all disciplines — show absolutely no vestige of those things which today we marvel at in this Mercury and the Sibyls. (3) Because it was solemn in the first times of the church, with a good end, to invent false books, that the new doctrine might more easily be admitted by the gentiles' wise men — of which Pope Gelasius in his decree and that of the Roman council enumerates and by best right condemns very many. And into this census are to be referred those Sibylline oracles which explain the secrets of our religion more openly than was ever done by God's prophets; likewise the whole book which under the name of Mercury Trismegistus began some centuries ago to be circulated, pseudepigraphically falsely inscribed — for it is the mere fiction of some Christian or rather semi-Christian, as our Casaubon from the matter and diction solidly demonstrates in many places. (4) Because writings of this sort, as soon as they came forth, were suspect to very many. For most truly blessed Augustine (City of God book 18, chapter 47): Whatever prophecies of others concerning God's grace through Christ Jesus are brought forth can be thought to have been fabricated by Christians. Therefore nothing is firmer for convincing any aliens, if they contend about this matter, and for supporting our own, if they have thought rightly, than that those divine predictions concerning Christ be brought forth which are written in the Jews' codices.

source_text: IX. Sunt autem hic notandae regulae. 1. Mysteria fidei non e naturae favissis, sed scripturarum paginis eruenda sunt, ut S.S. Trinitas, incarnatio filii Dei, electio ad salutem, redemtio, baptismus, S. coena & similia. Nam in his locum habet illud: Athenae nihil commune habent cum Hierosolymis; & illud Pauli Gal. 1.v.15. continuo non contuli cum carne & sanguine; & 2. Cor. 10.v.5. captivam ducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo. Neque enim facimus cum Raymundo Lullio & Albertino, quorum ille omnes articulos fidei, hic vero omnes conclusiones philosophicis principiis deducere satagit; multo minus cum Photinianis, qui rationem humanam in controversiis fidei passim habere videntur ante sacram scripturam: quantumvis hanc scabiem quidam nobis affricare conentur. Nam discrimen analyticae & dialecticae tractationis jure merito observamus: & analyticam probationem in Theologia vocamus spirituale ac Theologiae proprium principium theopneuston, divinitus revelatum ad demonstrationem seu confirmationem articulorum fidei, quibus salus nostra continetur, accommodatum. Et judicamus eum revera solum dici posse in Theologia analyticum, sive verum ac solidum Theologum, qui probationes suas & probationum principia deducit ex limpidissimis fontibus sacrarum literarum, aut ex iis, quae per sacras scripturas demonstrata sunt, nec quicquam alienum aut peregrinum ex philosophia vel hominum traditionibus, vel patrum testimoniis, nisi haec omnino cum sacris literis consentiant, aut ad veram sacrae scripturae interpretationem pertineant, admisceri patitur, tunc maxime, quando spiritualibus opus est demonstrationibus.
english: IX. And here rules are to be noted. 1. The mysteries of faith are to be dug out not from nature's storehouses, but from the pages of the Scriptures — such as the most holy Trinity, the incarnation of the Son of God, election to salvation, redemption, baptism, the Lord's Supper, and the like. For in these that [saying] has place: Athens has nothing in common with Jerusalem; and that of Paul ([[Galatians 1:15 >> Bible:Galatians 1:15]]), I did not immediately confer with flesh and blood; and ([[2 Corinthians 10:5 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 10:5]]), we take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.

For we do not side with Raymond Lull and Albertinus — of whom the former strives to deduce all articles of faith, the latter all conclusions, from philosophical principles — much less with the Photinians, who seem everywhere to hold human reason in controversies of faith before Sacred Scripture, however much some try to rub this itch onto us.

For we rightly and deservedly observe the distinction of analytic and dialectic treatment: and we call analytic proof in theology the spiritual principle proper to theology, theopneuston, divinely revealed, accommodated to the demonstration or confirmation of the articles of faith in which our salvation is contained. And we judge that he alone can truly be called analytic in theology — that is, a true and solid theologian — who draws his proofs and the principles of his proofs from the clearest springs of the sacred letters, or from those things which have been demonstrated through the Sacred Scriptures, and does not allow anything alien or foreign from philosophy or human traditions or the fathers' testimonies to be mixed in, unless these entirely agree with the sacred letters or pertain to the true interpretation of Sacred Scripture — and that especially when spiritual demonstrations are needed.

source_text: II. Estque vel ecclesiae testimonium, vel eorum qui sunt extra ecclesiam. III. Ecclesiae testimonium est primo purum aut mixtum. IV. Purum est, quod voce Ecclesiae rem credendam e solis scripturis definit. V. Mixtum est, quod voce Ecclesiae rem e scriptura & natura simul determinat. Sunt enim res quaedam in Theologia, quae partim per scripturam, partim per naturam innotescunt: ut, esse Deum; esse providentiam; esse magistratum; esse conjugium. Hic fides etiam naturalibus principiis potest firmari juxta illud: Vertite oculos ad volatilia coeli, & cognoscite lilia agri, Matth. 6.v.26. quarum etiam rerum Paulus meminit, Act. 14.v.17. Rom. 1.v.19. Quid, inquis, annon ex sola scriptura tum themata, tum argumenta theologica petuntur? Resp. Argumenta fidem Christianam fundantia, quibus nitimur, merito a sola scriptura ducuntur: illustrantia vero, quibus quovis modo utimur & juvamur, praesertim in refutatione haereseon & additionum humanarum, quibus necessario contradicimus, possunt etiam ex natura, recta ratione & humanis testimoniis ad hominem non incommode peti. Vide Chemnitium parte I. L. Theologic. de creatione cap. 3.
english: II. And it is either the Church's testimony, or that of those who are outside the Church. III. The Church's testimony is first pure or mixed. IV. Pure is that which by the Church's voice defines the matter to be believed from the Scriptures alone. V. Mixed is that which by the Church's voice determines the matter from Scripture and nature together.

For there are certain things in theology which become known partly through Scripture, partly through nature: for example, that God is; that there is providence; that there is a magistrate; that there is marriage. Here faith can also be confirmed by natural principles, according to that [saying]: Turn your eyes to the birds of the sky, and consider the lilies of the field ([[Matthew 6:26 >> Bible:Matthew 6:26]]) — of which things Paul also makes mention ([[Acts 14:17 >> Bible:Acts 14:17]]; [[Romans 1:19 >> Bible:Romans 1:19]]).

What then, you ask — are not both theological themes and arguments sought from Scripture alone? Reply: Arguments that found the Christian faith, on which we rest, are rightly drawn from Scripture alone; but illustratives, which we use and are helped by in any way — especially in refuting heresies and human additions, which we necessarily contradict — can also without inconvenience be sought from nature, right reason, and human testimonies ad hominem. See Chemnitz, Theological Commonplaces part I, on creation, chapter 3.

source_text: XIII. Fidelis relatio fit per publicum Ecclesiae scriptum. Huc pertinent tria symbola catholica, Apostolicum, Nicenum, Athanasianum. Deinde huc referri possunt Augustana confessio, confessio Gallica, Anglicana, Helvetica, Harmonia confessionum Euangelicarum, Catechesis Heidelbergensis cum similibus publicis scriptis. XIV. Privatum est, quod orthodoxus aliquis doctor publici juris fecit, non publico Ecclesiae, sed suo nomine. Hujus census sunt, Scripta pleraque Lutheri, Melanchthonis, Calvini, Bullingeri, Musculi, Chemnitii, Hemmingii, Martyris, Bezae, Ursini, Zanchii, B. Aretii, F. Junii, D. Parei, Whitakeri, Perkinsi, Polani, Piscatoris, & similium: imo & priscorum patrum tam Latinorum, quam Graecorum.
english: XIII. Faithful relation takes place through a public writing of the Church. Here pertain the three catholic symbols — the Apostolic, Nicene, Athanasian. Then here can be referred the Augsburg Confession, the Gallican, Anglican, Helvetic confessions, the Harmony of Evangelical Confessions, the Heidelberg Catechism, with similar public writings.

XIV. Private is that which some orthodox doctor has made of public right, not in the Church's public name, but in his own. Of this rank are most of the writings of Luther, Melanchthon, Calvin, Bullinger, Musculus, Chemnitz, Hemmingius, Martyr, Beza, Ursinus, Zanchi, Benedictus Aretius, Franciscus Junius, David Pareus, Whitaker, Perkins, Polanus, Piscator, and the like — indeed also of the ancient fathers, Latin as well as Greek.

source_text: VI. Estque hoc principium probatio aut declaratio. VII. Probatio est, qua aliquid esse tam e natura, quam ex scriptura evincitur, sic Deum esse tam natura, quam scriptura liber afferit, Esa. 41.v.22. ps. 19.v.2. VIII. Declaratio est, qua aliquid a scriptura propositum e natura declaratur. Sic Damascenus filii Dei generationem e natura declarat lib. 1. Orthodox. fid. c. 9. Quemadmodum, inquiens, lux ab igne semper gignitur, semperque in ipso est, & nequaquam separatur ab eo: hunc in modum & filius a patre gignitur, & nequaquam ab eo separatur, sed semper in eo est.
english: VI. And this principle is proof or declaration. VII. Proof is that by which something is shown to be both from nature and from Scripture — thus that God is, nature as well as the free Scripture asserts ([[Isaiah 41:22 >> Bible:Isaiah 41:22]]; [[Psalm 19:2 >> Bible:Psalm 19:2]]).

VIII. Declaration is that by which something proposed by Scripture is declared from nature. Thus Damascene declares the generation of the Son of God from nature (On the Orthodox Faith book 1, chapter 9): Just as, he says, light is always begotten from fire, and always is in it, and is by no means separated from it — in this way also the Son is begotten from the Father, and is by no means separated from him, but always is in him.
